Header: Maruca vitrata or Crochiphora testulalis Legume pod borer, bean pod borer, lima bean pod borer, mung moth, maruca

Prevention: Plant early to avoid the period of heavy infestation.
Use resistant/tolerant varieties and/or early maturing varieties if they are available.
Deep plough and harrow to kill larvae/ pupae or expose them to direct sunlight and predators.
Intercrop cowpeas with sorghum or maize to reduce the populations of the pod boring pests.
Remove weeds and alternate hosts, such as other leguminous plants, and destroy volunteer cowpea plants because they may harbor the borer.
Do not plant crop on the same piece of land for more than two seasons (rotate cowpea with maize or another non-host).
Monitoring: Monitoring
Additional relevant crops: common beans, kudzu, lima beans, soybean, cowpeas, lablab, green gram and wild leguminous plants such as
Mucuna .
Visit the field every day after flowering to look for signs of damage.
Check adult population using pheromone traps.
Place about 4 weeks after sowing cowpea and check at least 3 times a week.
When there is an average of two adults per trap take action.
Also, take action when 5 plants are damaged.
Cowpeas can be attacked by the legume pod borer from early budding through to harvest.
Look out for:
Flowers: presence of larvae (open the flowers to see them) and round holes.
Leaves: folded and stuck together.
Pods:
A distinct hole where larva entered.
Yellowish-brown balls on the outside (larvae faeces).
Eggs:
Single or in small groups.
On the flowers or flower buds and on the terminal shoots of young plants.
Oval, clear and light yellowish-white in colour; a single egg looks like a small drop of water.
Larvae/caterpillars: 17-20 mm long.
Whitish/pale green in colour with irregular brown-black spots.
Head is dark brown.
Feed on flowers and foliage.
Older larva feed on and bore into the pods.
Pupates beneath plant litter.
Adult/moth:
Wings are blackish-brown with white markings on the forewings and a wingspan of 20-25 mm.
Active at night.
During the day they rest on the undersides of leaves.
Direct Control: For small infestations, hand-pick eggs and larvae from the plants and crush them.
Prune leaves with white silk threads that stick together and also remove older leaves to allow more sunlight to reach the leaves and stems of the plants.
Neem products have proven to be effective against the larvae and are more cost-effective than synthetic insecticides.
Pod borers are difficult to control with insecticides because they remain hidden in the pod/bean.
